newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian army votes on constitution, bomb explodes.
newsitem.headline: Algerian army votes on constitution, bomb explodes.

text.p: A bomb exploded at a bus shelter in a town south of Algiers on Monday as over 500,000 members of Algeria's security forces began voting on a draft constitution that would bar Islamist parties from elections.

The security forces, in a statement carried by the official APS news agency, said one man was killed and 13 wounded -- six seriously -- when a bomb ripped through a bus shelter near the hospital in Berrouaghia.

The statement did not say who was responsible for the midday blast in the town 70 km (45 miles) south of Algiers. But it came as Algeria prepared for a national referendum on Thursday on constitutional changes that would bar people from seeking election as Islamic candidates.

The early vote for security forces, which also applied to bedouin scattered in remote areas, will free the military to protect voters against Moslem guerrillas when the national vote is held. The Armed Islamic Group warned people this week not to vote.

Algerian newspapers dubbed this the "Month of all horrors". Although the government insists the poll will be held in "full freedom and tranquility," more than 120 people have been killed in the past six weeks, according to independent sources in Algiers.

Government officials and their backers have stepped up a campaign for the constitutional changes. The draft, if approved by a majority of the 16.4 million electorate who vote, will broaden the president's paramount powers but limit him to two five-year terms.

It bans politicians from campaigning as representatives of Islam or the Arab or Berber communities. Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia said on Sunday during a campaign rally in Algiers the draft constitution aims to strengthen a multiparty democracy in a united nation.

Algerian expatriates in Europe and other Arab countries also were voting. Algerian state television showed voters lining up in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Brussels and Bonn. Voters said they were pained by the killing at home and hoped their vote would help restore peace.

Officials said television images in last year's presidential vote of expatriates flooding polling stations despite snow and heavy rain encouraged voters at home to turn up in defiance of Moslem guerrilla death threats.

Secular opposition firebrand Said Saadi, casting doubt on the fairness of the election, told the Algerian Liberte newspaper that national authorities had urged Algiers' local officials to "ban the slighest (independent) presence in the offices where the ballots will be counted."
Despite reports of tighter security, at least in large urban centres, violence in Algeria continued unabated in the days before the poll.

A car bomb killed five people and wounded 19 on Sunday in the central garrison town of Blida, newspapers said on Monday. Security forces killed nine guerrillas in two operations in the previous 24 hours near Algiers, newspapers also reported.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead.
